title: He cooked breakfast…
paragraphs:
He cooked breakfast…
for the man who denied Him.

Because this wasn’t just a meal.
This was a moment that should not exist.

Three times he said, “I don’t know Him.”
Not once.
Not twice.
Three.

With curses.
With fear.
With distance.
Luke records it—“The Lord turned and looked at Peter…” (Luke 22:61)

Not anger.
Not shock.
But truth.

The cross is behind them.
The tomb is empty.
Jesus is alive.
So what does a man do when he can’t face his failure?

Back to fishing.
Back to the old life.
Back to the version of himself that didn’t carry this kind of guilt.

“You had your chance.”
“You blew it.”
“God is done with you.”
And maybe you know that voice.

That private guilt.
That hidden compromise.
That thing no one knows… but you do.

You still worship.
You still show up.
But deep inside—
Empty nets dragging behind tired men.
And a voice cuts through the silence:
“Cast the net on the right side.”

“If that’s Jesus…
there’s still hope for me.”
Because this will change how you see God.
Jesus is not holding a sermon.
He’s not holding a list of Peter’s failures.
He’s not even asking questions yet.
“When they got out on land, they saw a charcoal fire in place, with fish laid out on it, and bread.” (John 21:9)
The only other time that phrase appears in Scripture?
Jesus recreates the scene of Peter’s worst failure.
This is how Jesus deals with shame.
The smell of mercy in the air.
“Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” (John 21:15)
Because Peter denied Him three times.
Jesus is not rubbing it in.
Every question is a stitch in a torn soul.
Every response is a step back into calling.

“Feed my lambs.”
“Tend my sheep.”
“Feed my sheep.”

“You’re not finished.”
“You’re not disqualified.”
“I still choose you.”
But that Jesus meets you after you do.

Romans 5:8 says,
“God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after you clean your record.
While you were still in it.

And Acts 3:19 says,
“Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out.”
Jesus didn’t cook that breakfast casually.
Your denial… your compromise… your hidden life—
But it is not greater than the cross.
“I’ll come back to God when I’m better.”
You come back because you’re not.
Peter didn’t clean himself up before jumping into that water.

Not your image.
Not your reputation.
Not your comfort.
Because repentance is not just saying sorry.
It’s coming back to the fire.
It’s letting Him rewrite the moment you thought defined you.
You are not your worst night.
You are not your loudest failure.
You are not the voice in your head that says “too late.”
Let Him give you purpose again.
“We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.”
